title: Grupo Coppel walkthrough
name: coppel-walkthrough
chapters: Six pods, no one between them

text: Hi, I'm Tucker. This is a short walk through my fourteen months with Grupo Coppel, one of Mexico's largest retailers, as a founding member of their Digital Center of Excellence.

When I joined, the design team was handing work to a development partner, a team from my own company. They were reviewing it from a single screenshot in Jira, not the full set of states and components the designers had built.
In that role I was there for Coppel and for that team, so I made it clear the work gets reviewed in full.
Leadership wanted design on par with the best tech companies. The more I looked, the more I saw each group only seeing its own piece of the customer.
Product was a good example. Their personas were really buyer personas, built around spending and financing.

My product counterpart and I brought product managers, some of our UX designers and someone from development together to rebuild them around needs, the jobs people were trying to get done, and how they felt.
Then we walked those personas through a journey workshop. By the end, everyone in the room really saw the value, and they'd found gaps they'd never looked for.
There's no metric on it, but the product one-pagers that came after were noticeably better.

On the design side, a skills-gap assessment showed how much room there was to grow. I rewrote most of the job descriptions so leaders were craft experts with time to mentor, and I sat on the panel that hired senior managers against them.
The assessment also showed a structural problem. Six pods each owned one phase, and nobody owned the handoffs between them.
And design reported to delivery, not outcomes, so requirements showed up as decisions already made.
I talked it through with product and technology first, then recommended organizing by channel, the way engineering already was, with a guild owning the whole experience.
Leadership agreed, and then it was put on hold behind a CEO-led redesign.
What lasted came from the team. In a day-and-a-half workshop, they wrote their own five design principles, and those are still in Coppel's design system.
I also made the case for a human-in-the-loop process with AI, from product to design.
Honestly, the tools weren't good enough yet for me to prove it out, but I was confident they'd get there quickly, and they did.
Looking back, I think it was the same problem at every level. Each group only saw its own piece, and getting people to see the whole moved things fastest.
I used AI to write the team's mobile guidelines, and looking at them now, they'd make a great set of files for an AI coding process.
